```{r}
#| include: false
source("_common.R")
```

# Functions and Operators {#sec-func}

Every audit check we run on data does the same small job again and again. Convert an amount to lakh. Work out the GST on a bill. Find the percentage change in a district's expenditure over last year. Total a column while leaving out the missing values. In R, each such job is done by a *function*. Most of the functions we need are already in R. When one is missing, we can write it ourselves in a few lines, test it once, and use it in every audit.

In this chapter we learn what a function is, how to read its arguments and defaults, and how to write our own. A silent default can change an audit total, so we pay attention to defaults throughout. We end with a few small functions that every auditor will find useful.

What is a function? Mathematically, a function $f$ is a rule which maps an input $x$ to a specific output, denoted $f(x)$. Every input must have an output, and the same input must give the same output every time. So if $x=y$, then $f(x)=f(y)$.

```{r echo=FALSE, fig.show='hold', fig.align='center', fig.cap="Author's illustration of a function", out.width="99%"}
knitr::include_graphics("images/function.png")
```

For example, *squaring* a number is a function, written $f(x)=x^2$. So is the *square root* of a positive number.

A function may have more than one input. Suppose a function adds three times `x`, one time `y` and two times `z`. We write it as $f(x,y,z) = 3x+y+2z$. In programming, the inputs are called *arguments*. Usually the user gives their values, but many arguments have a *default* value, which the function uses silently if no value is given.

R calculates the output as per the definition of the function. If the output is assigned to an object, nothing is printed. Otherwise, the output is usually printed in the console. (Some functions do their work silently, like saving a file, and return nothing visible.)

Every programming language comes with ready-made functions. In this chapter we will see how to use them, and how to write our own, in @sec-cust. The next chapter lists the most useful built-in ones.

As an example, `sum()` is a built-in function, which adds up all the numbers given to it. Here it totals the amounts of two batches of bills.
```{r}
sum(c(45000, 12500, 9800), c(62000, 18750))
```

To see the arguments of a function, we can use the function `args()`, which takes a _function name_ and returns its arguments.
```{r}
args(sum)
```

We see an argument `na.rm`, with the default value `FALSE`. Unless we say otherwise, the function uses this default silently, and a single missing value makes the whole sum missing. If we want missing values left out, we must say `na.rm = TRUE` explicitly.
```{r}
sum(c(45000, 12500, NA, 9800))
sum(c(45000, 12500, NA, 9800), na.rm = TRUE)
```


To see the code of a function, type its name without parentheses in the console. (For `sum()`, the work is done by compiled code inside R, so we only see a short stub.)

```{r}
sum
```

For more help on any existing function, see @sec-help.

## Custom functions {#sec-cust}

One of R's greatest strengths is that users can write their own functions\index{custom function}. In fact, many of the functions in R are built from other functions. If you find yourself copying the same few lines of code again and again, changing only a value or two, it is time to write a function. The structure of a function looks like this:

```
myfunctionname <- function(arg1, arg2, ... ){
  statements
  return(object)
}
```
Objects created inside a function are local to it. The object returned can be of any type, from a single value to a list. If there is no `return()`, the function returns the value of its last line, which is the usual style in R.

Let us take an example. We create a function which takes 3 numbers, and adds three times the first, the second, and twice the third.
```{r}
my_fun1 <- function(first,second,third){
  first*3+second+third*2
}
# let us check whether it works as desired
my_fun1(3,1,10)
```
- If the arguments are not named, they are taken in the order in which they are defined.
- Named arguments can be given in any order.
```{r}
my_fun1(second=3, first=1, third=10)
```
- Partial names are also matched.
```{r}
my_fun1(sec=3,fir=1,thi=10)
```
  This works, but avoid it in code you keep. A partial name may match a different argument if the function is changed later.
- We can give default values to any argument. The default is used only when no value is given. See this example.
```{r}
# a function which adds twice the second argument to the first
# the first argument is 10 by default
my_fun2 <- function(first=10, second){
  first+second*2
}
my_fun2(second = 10)
my_fun2(1, 10)
```
- A function may need no argument at all.
```{r}
my_fun3 <- function(){
  print('Hi')
}
my_fun3()
```

### Special argument ellipsis `...` {-}

In the help of a function, you may have come across something like `sum(..., na.rm = FALSE)`. The three dots `...`\index{... ellipsis} are called the *ellipsis*\index{ellipsis}. They mean that the function can take any number of arguments in their place.

The point to note is that any argument which comes *after* `...` must be given by name. See this example.
```{r}
sum(1:100, NA, TRUE)
sum(1:100, NA, na.rm = TRUE)
```
In the first line, `TRUE` was not taken as the value of `na.rm`. It became one more number to add, as `1`, so the result is still `NA`. Only the named `na.rm = TRUE` works.

We can use the three dots in our own functions too. Inside the function, `list(...)` collects whatever was passed. See this simple example.
```{r}
my_ellipsis_func <- function(...){
  l <- list(...) # unpack ellipsis
  length(l) # return length of l
}
my_ellipsis_func(1:10, 11:20, 'a string') # we are passing three arguments
```

### Environment issues {-}

- A function works on its own copies of the arguments. Changing them inside the function does not change anything in the global environment\index{global environment}.
```{r}
x <- 10
my_fun4 <- function(x){
  x*2
}
my_fun4(2)
x
```
- An object created inside a function is not available outside it, even if it has the same name as an object outside.
```{r}
y <- 5
my_fun5 <- function(){
  y <- 1
  return(y)
}
my_fun5()
y
```
- To create or change an object outside the function deliberately, there is the *super-assignment* operator `<<-`.
```{r}
y <- 5
my_fun5 <- function(){
  y <<- 1
  return(y)
}
my_fun5()
y
```
  Use `<<-` rarely, if ever. A function which changes things outside itself is hard to follow and to check. It is better for a function to *return* its result, which is then assigned.
- As already stated, a function can return an object of any type. Here it returns a list, with a few summary figures of a set of bill amounts.
```{r}
my_list_fun <- function(x){
  list(sum=sum(x),
       mean = mean(x),
       sd = sd(x))
}
my_list_fun(c(45000, 12500, 9800, 62000, 18750))
```

### Short functions with `\(x)` {-}

Since R 4.1, a short function can be written with a backslash in place of the word `function`. So `\(x) x * 2` is the same as `function(x) x * 2`. Such *anonymous* functions, which are not given a name, are handy inside other functions, as we will see in @sec-purrr and later chapters.

```{r}
(\(x) x * 2)(21)
```

## Audit use case, a small toolkit of audit functions {#sec-func-audit}

Let us write three small functions which come in handy in audit analysis. Each is a few lines long, and each is tested on figures whose answer we already know.

**Amounts in lakh.** Reports in India often show amounts in lakh or crore.

```{r}
in_lakh <- function(x, digits = 2) {
  round(x / 1e5, digits)
}
in_lakh(c(1250000, 87500, 31415926))
in_lakh(31415926, digits = 0)
```

**Percentage change.** Comparing a figure with the previous year is an everyday task. Here are the expenditures of three districts on a scheme, in ₹ lakh, for two years.

```{r}
pct_change <- function(old, new, digits = 1) {
  round(100 * (new - old) / old, digits)
}
pct_change(old = c(Alwar = 120, Bharatpur = 80, Churu = 50),
           new = c(Alwar = 150, Bharatpur = 60, Churu = 50))
```

Since R works on whole vectors, the function works on all three districts at once, without any extra code. Alwar's expenditure rose by a quarter, Bharatpur's fell by a quarter, and Churu's did not change. A large rise or fall is a reason to ask the district for an explanation.

::: callout-warning
## Caution
If the old figure is zero, `pct_change()` divides by zero. The result is then `Inf`, or `NaN` when both figures are zero. Such results are not percentages. Look at those cases separately before you summarise the changes.
:::

**Checking the input.** A function used often should stop with a clear message when given wrong input, rather than return a wrong answer. `stopifnot()` does this simply.

```{r error=TRUE}
gst_amount <- function(taxable_value, rate = 18) {
  stopifnot(is.numeric(taxable_value), rate %in% c(0, 5, 18, 40))  # main GST rates since 22 September 2025
  round(taxable_value * rate / 100, 2)
}
gst_amount(c(1000, 2500))
gst_amount(1000, rate = 15)
```

::: callout-tip
## Audit tip

Put your frequently used functions, like these, in one `.R` file, say `audit_functions.R`, and load them at the start of every analysis with `source("audit_functions.R")`. The same tested code is then used across all your audits, and a correction made once applies everywhere.
:::

## A suggested workflow

When the same few lines of code keep coming back in your audit work, follow these steps.

1.  **Spot the repetition.** If you copy the same lines again and again, changing only a value or two, turn them into a function.
2.  **Know the defaults.** Use `args()` to see the arguments of a function and their defaults, like `na.rm = FALSE` in `sum()`. A silent default can change a total.
3.  **Write a small function.** Give it a clear name, like `in_lakh()`. Give sensible defaults, such as the number of digits.
4.  **Test it on known values.** Try the function on a few amounts whose answer you already know, before using it on the full register.
5.  **Check the input.** Add `stopifnot()`, so that the function stops with a clear error on wrong input, like a GST rate that does not exist.
6.  **Return the result.** Let the function return its result, and assign it outside. Avoid `<<-`, which changes things outside the function and is hard to check.
7.  **Keep functions in one file.** Save tested functions in one file, like `audit_functions.R`, and load them with `source()` at the start of every analysis.

::: callout-important
## Remember

A function is only as good as its testing. Check it on values whose answer you know, and make it stop on wrong input with `stopifnot()`. A function that quietly returns a wrong answer is worse than one that gives an error.
:::

## Summary of functions used

| Function | Package | What it does |
|-----------------------|----------------|--------------------------------|
| `function()`, `\()` | base R | Create a function |
| `return()` | base R | Return a value from a function (otherwise the last value is returned) |
| `args()` | base R | Show the arguments of a function |
| `...` | base R | Pass any number of arguments |
| `<<-` | base R | Assign to an object outside the function (use rarely) |
| `stopifnot()` | base R | Stop with an error if a condition is not met |
| `source()` | base R | Run the code in an R file, like a file of your functions |
| `sum()`, `mean()`, `sd()`, `round()` | base R | Total, average, standard deviation and rounding, used inside our functions |
| `print()` | base R | Print a value |
